Additional scope from the live `gpt-5.5` review:

- Distinguish **API-equivalent estimate** from **actual subscription spend**. A ChatGPT Pro subscription, OpenAI API key, OpenRouter key, and provider/account-specific billing can have different economics even for the same underlying model.
- Treat coding-agent harnesses separately from model providers. Example: Hermes may run `gpt-5.5` through an OpenAI/Codex provider path, so pricing should resolve through the provider/model, not through the Hermes tool name.
- Add a pricing/billing basis field that can distinguish at least:
  - public API/OpenRouter estimate
  - provider/account/API-key-specific price
  - session-reported actual/estimated cost
  - subscription-included or subscription-unknown
  - unpriced/unmapped
- For subscription-backed use, avoid presenting public API token pricing as the user's actual bill. The UI should say `API-equivalent estimate` unless actual provider billing is confirmed.

## UX Alternatives To Choose From

These keep the mechanic simple while giving the update action a clear product feel instead of a generic admin button.

### Option A: Footer Utility Chip

**Tone:** industrial/utilitarian, compact, command-center style.

Place a small status chip in the existing footer beside `active sources` and `last updated`.

Example copy:

```text
app: main@a1b2c3d clean · Update App
```

Interaction:

- `Update App` is a compact button/chip.
- Click opens a tiny confirmation popover: `Pull latest and sync dependencies?`
- Running state: `Updating...`
- Success: `Updated to d4e5f6a. Restart required.`
- Dirty state: `Local changes detected. Update manually.`

Pros:

- Smallest UI change.
- Keeps update near operational status metadata.
- Least visual noise on the dashboard.

Cons:

- Easy to miss.
- Footer can become dense on mobile.

Best if we want the safest first iteration.

### Option B: Settings Maintenance Card

**Tone:** refined/minimal, deliberate admin control.

Add a `Maintenance` card to `/settings` with version details and the update action.

Example layout:

```text
Maintenance
Current version  main@a1b2c3d
Worktree         clean
Upstream         origin/main

[Update App]
```

Interaction:

- Button runs the update endpoint directly after a short confirmation.
- Result appears inside the card as a persistent status line.
- Include fallback command on failure: `git pull --ff-only && uv sync`.

Pros:

- Cleanest information architecture.
- Keeps risky actions away from the main analytics dashboard.
- Easier to make accessible and readable.

Cons:

- One extra click to reach it.
- Less discoverable than footer placement.

Best if we want the most maintainable UX.

### Option C: Header Status Rail

**Tone:** dashboard cockpit, slightly more prominent.

Add a thin app status rail above the Overview title.

Example copy:

```text
Dashboard build main@a1b2c3d · clean · last checked 2m ago     [Update]
```

Interaction:

- `Update` button stays visible near the top.
- When update starts, the rail expands into an inline progress/status row.
- Success keeps the status visible until page refresh: `Restart dashboard to activate latest version.`

Pros:

- Very discoverable.
- Makes version provenance explicit.
- Good place for future app-health status if needed.

Cons:

- Adds visual weight to the main dashboard.
- Slightly broader UI change.

Best if version/update status should be part of the dashboard’s main operational story.

### Option D: Command Palette Style Modal

**Tone:** retro-terminal/operator console.

Use a small `Update App` button in Settings or footer, but clicking opens a command-style modal.

Example modal:

```text
> update app
Checking worktree... clean
Pulling origin/main... fast-forward only
Syncing uv environment...
Restart required
```

Interaction:

- Shows command phases as read-only log lines.
- Keeps raw output collapsed behind `Show details`.
- Escape closes only after completion/failure.

Pros:

- Memorable and on-brand for local developer tooling.
- Makes the mechanic transparent without feeling like a generic toast.
- Useful for debugging failures.

Cons:

- More UI code than needed for v1.
- Modal behavior needs careful keyboard/focus handling.

Best if we want a distinctive experience and are okay with slightly more implementation effort.

## Recommendation

Start with **Option B: Settings Maintenance Card**.

It is the best balance of simple, safe, and clear. This is a potentially risky local operation, so it belongs in Settings rather than competing with usage analytics. If we want more discoverability later, add a small footer version chip that links to the Settings card.

## Suggested V1 Decision

Implement:

- Settings `Maintenance` card.
- `GET /api/app-version` on Settings page load.
- `POST /api/update` from the card.
- Conservative states: clean, dirty, updating, success, already-current, failed.
- No auto-restart.

Defer:

- Modal command log.
- Header rail.
- Background scheduled update checks.
- Branch switching or auto-stash.

---

## Goal

Make dashboard loading and refresh behavior visible, predictable, and accessible without masking the underlying performance work.

## Scope

This roadmap coordinates three related lanes:

- loading, empty, error, and retry states across cards, chart, model breakdown, and usage history;
- measured endpoint performance and request lifecycle improvements;
- the product decision for the initial homepage range.

## Child issues

- [#12 — Standardize dashboard loading, empty, and error states](https://github.com/raychrisgdp/coding-agent-usage-dashboard/issues/12)
- [#24 — Profile and reduce dashboard endpoint load time](https://github.com/raychrisgdp/coding-agent-usage-dashboard/issues/24)
- [#36 — Default homepage range to 7 days for faster initial load](https://github.com/raychrisgdp/coding-agent-usage-dashboard/issues/36)

## Work boundaries

- #12 owns the visible UI state contract: section-local loading, empty, error, retry, and accessibility behavior.
- #24 owns profiling and performance changes: query cost, aggregation reuse, caching, request cancellation, and refresh latency.
- #36 owns the initial-range product choice. It may proceed independently of performance profiling; changing the default range does not replace fixing 30-day latency.
- [#17](https://github.com/raychrisgdp/coding-agent-usage-dashboard/issues/17) remains a separate chart/input/focus accessibility issue.
- [#18](https://github.com/raychrisgdp/coding-agent-usage-dashboard/issues/18) remains a separate mobile-layout and reduced-motion issue, with loading animation behavior treated as a cross-cutting constraint.

## Integration rule

Performance work may change request timing or cancellation behavior, but its frontend loading behavior must conform to the state contract in #12. Prefer parallel implementation where contracts permit; use a convergence review before calling the roadmap complete.

## Done when

- All affected dashboard sections expose visible loading, empty, error, and retry states.
- Refreshes preserve useful existing data where appropriate and prevent stale responses from overwriting newer selections.
- 30-day latency has measured before/after evidence or a documented reason no optimization was made.
- The initial range decision is implemented or explicitly deferred.
- Reduced-motion, keyboard, screen-reader, and narrow-screen behavior remain covered by the related issues.
- Full local tests and browser smoke verification pass.

## Non-goals

- This roadmap does not redesign chart filtering; that work is tracked by [#9](https://github.com/raychrisgdp/coding-agent-usage-dashboard/issues/9) and its child issues.
- This roadmap does not change token accounting or pricing semantics.

## Summary

The model breakdown misclassifies Codex CLI sessions that use the OpenCode Go plugin and assigns an unsupported price to DeepSeek V4 Flash.

## Current behavior

- Codex stores the plugin model as `model_provider=openai` with model ID `opencode-go/deepseek-v4-flash`.
- The dashboard displays it as an OpenAI model instead of OpenCode Go.
- Non-free `deepseek-v4-flash` receives a price from the hardcoded/OpenRouter pricing path even though no trusted provider rate is configured.

## Expected behavior

- Decode `opencode-go/<model>` and `opencode-free/<model>` namespaces from Codex model IDs.
- Display the provider as OpenCode Go/OpenCode Free rather than OpenAI.
- Keep non-free DeepSeek V4 Flash unpriced until a trusted rate is available.
- Keep the explicit `deepseek-v4-flash-free` variant at zero cost.

## Validation

- Add regression coverage for Codex provider normalization.
- Add regression coverage for paid DeepSeek V4 Flash remaining unpriced even when remote pricing is present.
- Add regression coverage for the explicit free variant.

> Original GitHub timestamps, author identity, reactions, and timeline events are preserved in the private raw archive.

---

## Problem

The dashboard currently centers range selection around `last N days` presets plus a custom numeric days box. That is fast, but it does not let users select an explicit date window such as `2026-06-01 → 2026-06-15`.

We should support explicit start/end dates while keeping the current quick presets.

## Desired UX

Add date range controls that support both workflows:

- quick presets: `3d`, `7d`, `30d`, `90d`, `All`
- custom numeric days: `N days`
- explicit date range: `Start date` and `End date`

Behavior:

- Selecting a preset fills the date inputs automatically.
  - Example: `7d` sets start/end to the computed last-7-days window.
- Entering `N` in the custom days box also fills start/end automatically.
  - Example: `45` sets `start = today - 44 days`, `end = today` using the dashboard’s current local-date convention.
- Editing either start or end date switches the active mode to explicit date range.
- Applying explicit dates updates overview, daily chart, model breakdown, and history consistently.
- If start/end are invalid, show an inline error and do not fetch.
- If `All` is selected, clear or disable explicit date inputs with clear copy.

## Implementation Notes

Current APIs are `days`-based. We need to decide the backend contract before changing UI behavior.

Suggested simple contract:

- Keep existing `days` support for presets and backwards compatibility.
- Add optional query params to relevant endpoints:
  - `start_date=YYYY-MM-DD`
  - `end_date=YYYY-MM-DD`
- If `start_date`/`end_date` are provided, they take precedence over `days`.
- Use one shared date-window parser/helper so overview/models/daily/history stay consistent.
- Keep source provenance and token semantics unchanged.

Likely endpoints affected:

- `/api/overview`
- `/api/models`
- `/api/daily`
- `/api/usage-history`

Likely frontend changes:

- `templates/index.html`
- range-control state management
- fetch URL construction
- active button/explicit-range state
- accessible labels for date inputs

## Acceptance Criteria

- Users can select an explicit start and end date from the homepage controls.
- Preset buttons still work as today.
- Entering custom `N days` automatically populates start/end.
- Editing start/end switches to explicit range mode.
- All dashboard sections use the same resolved date window.
- Invalid date ranges show a visible inline error.
- Existing `days` query behavior remains supported.
- Tests cover:
  - default range behavior
  - custom days filling start/end
  - explicit start/end precedence over days
  - invalid date range rejection
  - all affected endpoints using consistent boundaries.
issues.title: Support explicit start/end date range controls

## Context

## UX

- Add a small `Update App` control in the footer or Settings page, not as a primary dashboard CTA.
- Show app version details near the control:
  - current branch
  - short commit SHA
  - dirty/clean state
- Button states:
  - idle: `Update App`
  - running: disabled, `Updating...`
  - success: `Updated to <sha>. Restart the dashboard to use the latest version.`
  - already current: `Already up to date.`
  - local changes: `Local changes detected. Update manually to avoid overwriting work.`
  - failure: short error plus copyable fallback command: `git pull --ff-only && uv sync`

## Mechanic

Keep the first implementation conservative and server-side.

Add endpoints:

- `GET /api/app-version`
  - returns branch, current short SHA, upstream status if available, and dirty state
- `POST /api/update`
  - refuses when the worktree is dirty
  - refuses when no upstream branch exists
  - runs `git pull --ff-only`
  - runs `uv sync` after a successful pull
  - returns old SHA, new SHA, status, and short command output/error text

Implementation notes:

- Use `subprocess.run([...], cwd=repo_root, timeout=...)` with argument arrays, not shell strings.
- Do not run arbitrary browser-provided commands.
- Do not support branch switching from the UI.
- Do not auto-stash or overwrite local changes.
- Do not auto-restart in the first version.
- Use `POST`, not `GET`, for the update action.
- Because the app currently binds to `0.0.0.0`, restrict the update endpoint to localhost requests or clearly gate/document it as local/private only.

## Problem

This repo has good agent operating guidance in `AGENTS.md`, but it does not yet have a repo-local slash-command surface. The GDP SDK repo (`https://github.com/GDP-ADMIN/glaip-sdk/`) already has a mature `.agents/commands/` command system with provider adapters symlinked into Cursor/OpenCode/Windsurf/Copilot paths.

We should migrate the small, crucial subset into this repo so agents can use the same delivery workflow without copying the whole GDP command tree.

## Goal

Create a simplified `.agents/commands/` setup for this repo, adapted from `GDP-ADMIN/glaip-sdk`, with only the commands that matter for day-to-day issue-to-PR work.

## Commands to migrate and simplify

Primary commands:

- `/issue` — create/refine a GitHub issue from a problem statement; check existing issues first; keep scope small and linked to current repo context.
- `/goal` — end-to-end implementation loop for a ready issue/slice: plan, implement, validate, commit/push, create/update PR, run local review unless explicitly stopped.
- `/finish` — merge-readiness gate: verify review/checks/status, merge only when approved, then cleanup worktree/branch.
- `/review` — local repo-native PR/code review that writes `reviews/REVIEW_<branch>.md` using the repo's review format.

Required dependencies/helpers, but simplified:

- `_common-git-steps.md`
- `_common-github-steps.md`
- `_common-test-steps.md`
- `_common-review-workflow.md`
- `_common-review-report-format.md`
- `_common-closing-gate.md`
- `_goal-defaults.md`
- `_goal-cycle.md`
- `_goal-worker-dispatch.md` only if still needed after simplification
- `_finish-readiness-gates.md`
- any tiny command-local helpers needed by `/issue`, `/goal`, `/finish`, `/review`

Avoid migrating the full GDP command catalog. Do **not** copy commands like release, learn, cleanup, explain, update-specs, fix-integration, etc. unless they are strictly necessary for the four core commands above.

## Provider adapter paths

Canonical source should be:

```text
.agents/commands/
```

Provider adapters should symlink to the canonical source where supported:

```text
.cursor/commands -> ../.agents/commands
.opencode/command -> ../.agents/commands
.windsurf/workflows -> ../.agents/commands
.github/prompts -> ../.agents/commands
```

If a provider path already exists or has incompatible structure, document the decision instead of overwriting silently.

## Adaptation requirements

- Rewrite commands for this repo, not GDP SDK specifics.
- Keep commands short enough that an agent will actually follow them.
- Preserve the local worktree rule from this repo's `AGENTS.md`.
- Preserve the repo verification commands:

  uv run python -m unittest tests.test_app tests.test_readme -v

- `/goal` should not create large monolithic changes; it should respect small PRs and stop/ask when scope expands.
- `/issue` should not implement; it only creates/refines the issue and records next action.

---

## Problem
The dashboard can take multiple seconds to refresh the top cards, chart, model table, and usage history. PR 22 improved local loading feedback, but it did not address the underlying endpoint latency.

## Current Timing Evidence
Measured locally against `http://127.0.0.1:8321` on the PR 22 branch with live data, three sequential samples per endpoint:

| Endpoint | Samples | Best observed |
|---|---:|---:|
| `/api/overview?days=30` | 1530ms, 1467ms, 1450ms | 1450ms |
| `/api/models?days=30` | 1720ms, 1642ms, 1762ms | 1642ms |
| `/api/daily?days=30&top_n=8` | 1798ms, 12648ms, 4245ms | 1798ms |
| `/api/usage-history?limit=30` | 2947ms, 2927ms, 2967ms | 2927ms |

Page refresh currently launches multiple API requests, so total perceived loading can still feel slow even when they run in parallel.

## Suspected Bottleneck
Not fully proven yet; needs profiling. Current code strongly suggests duplicated aggregation work:

- `/api/overview`, `/api/models`, and `/api/daily` each run separate SQLite scans/aggregations over OpenCode `message.data` using repeated `json_extract(...)` calls.
- `/api/daily` also merges Codex/Hermes records after the OpenCode aggregation.
- `/api/usage-history` has its own recent-session query and merge path.
- The frontend calls these endpoints independently on range changes, so the same source data is parsed/aggregated several times for one dashboard refresh.

## Suggested Scope
- Add lightweight endpoint timing/profiling logs for local diagnostics.
- Use `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` and focused timing around OpenCode SQLite queries, Codex record loading, Hermes record loading, cost normalization/pricing, and JSON response shaping.
- Identify whether the slow path is SQLite JSON extraction, cross-source adapters, Python aggregation, response size, or repeated endpoint calls.
- Avoid guessing: document timings before and after any change.
- Consider one or more fixes after profiling:
  - per-range in-process cache for source aggregates
  - shared aggregate builder used by overview/models/daily
  - combined dashboard payload endpoint for initial load/range changes
  - narrower history endpoint work when only chart Top-N changes
  - SQLite indexes or generated/cached columns if JSON extraction is the limiting factor
  - request cancellation/debounce for repeated range/tab changes

## Acceptance Criteria
- A profiling note identifies the measured bottleneck(s), not just assumed causes.
- Dashboard refresh for 30d live data is materially faster, with before/after endpoint timings included in the PR.
- Top-N chart changes do not trigger unnecessary overview/model/history recomputation.
- Loading UX remains section-local and accessible; no full-screen shimmer/sweep.
- Existing tests and local browser smoke pass.

## Related
- #12 tracks standardized loading/empty/error states and per-area loading UX.
- PR #22 exposed the current latency and loading-state confusion while clarifying token-card semantics.

> Migration source: `raychrisgdp/coding-agent-usage-dashboard` issue #23
> Original author: `raychrisgdp`
> Created: `2026-06-02T06:29:20Z`
> Updated: `2026-06-11T11:29:12Z`
> Original state: `closed`
> Original URL: https://github.com/raychrisgdp/coding-agent-usage-dashboard/issues/23
> Original GitHub timestamps, author identity, reactions, and timeline events are preserved in the private raw archive.

---

## Summary

Turn the Overview from a neutral metrics report into a decision-guided usage dashboard: show what changed, what dominates, what is risky/partial, and what the user should inspect next.

This is intentionally a follow-up to #20 / PR #22. PR #22 should stay scoped to token-card naming, formulas, and cost-confidence visibility. This issue covers broader information architecture, chart interpretation, and source/model focus interactions.

## Current state

The page is clean, but it mostly reports raw data:

```text
Overview
Top cards show full token volume. Session totals and cache details appear in secondary lines.

Sessions | Total Tokens | Input Tokens | Output Tokens | API-Equivalent Cost
Tool Sources
Daily Tokens by Model
Model Breakdown
Usage History
```

Observed 30d live examples from the current dashboard:

```text
Total Tokens: 11.2B
Cached share: ~93%
Top source: OpenCode, 7.3B tokens
Top model: gpt-5.5 (openai), 50% of volume
Peak day: 2026-05-19, ~989.5M tokens
API-equivalent cost: ~$6.3K, partial estimate, 35/65 models priced
```

Those are the decision-relevant facts, but today they are scattered across cards, source tiles, chart legend, and table rows.

## Desired direction

Add a compact `Usage Summary` strip above the metric cards. The summary should answer:

- How much usage happened in the selected period?
- What source/tool dominates?
- What model dominates?
- Which day was the peak?
- Is the cost estimate complete or partial?
- What should the user inspect next?

Example copy:

```text
30d usage: 11.2B tokens · 93% cached · OpenCode leads · GPT-5.5 is 50% of volume
Peak day: May 19 · 989.5M tokens · Cost estimate partial: 35/65 models priced
```

## Proposed metric-card hierarchy

After the summary strip, the cards should support the story rather than compete equally.

Recommended order:

```text
Total Tokens
API-Equivalent Cost
Input Tokens
Output Tokens
Sessions
```

Rationale:

- `Sessions` is useful context, but too prominent as the first card for a token/cost dashboard.
- Cost is likely the most reactive number and should not be orphaned on a second row.
- `Input Tokens` and `Output Tokens` should remain paired.

If source mix is added, prefer showing it in the summary or Tool Sources section rather than as a peer metric card:

```text
Usage Summary strip:
OpenCode 65% · Codex 22% · Hermes 13%
```

## Tool Sources follow-up

Current source cards all say `ACTIVE SOURCE`, which makes selection state ambiguous.

Use explicit states:

```text
Included in totals
Click to focus chart
```

When selected:

```text
Focused
Showing chart + table for OpenCode
```

Acceptance details:

- source cards use real buttons/links for focus actions
- selected source has stronger visual treatment and `aria-pressed=true`
- unselected included sources are lower contrast but still visible
- if no source is selected, all sources say `Included in totals`

## Chart and legend follow-up

The stacked chart is useful, but the legend is currently mostly passive. Add decision cues and interactive focus states:

- clicking a legend item focuses/isolates the model
- selected model produces a summary above the chart
- selected source/model states clear each other predictably
- chart tooltip shows daily total plus top contributors
- chart marks peak day

Example focus summary:

```text
Focus: gpt-5.5 · 50% of 30d volume · peak May 19
```

Example annotation:

```text
Peak: May 19 · 989.5M tokens
```

## Typography and visual system

Move toward a Linear-style dark dashboard:

- keep saturated model/source colors
- use sans-serif for headings, labels, and explanatory copy
- use monospace only for numbers, model IDs, code paths, and compact table values
- keep metric values strong, but reduce terminal-dump heaviness in prose
- use subtle borders and dark surface luminance steps for hierarchy

## Non-goals

- Do not change token formulas from #20 / PR #22.
- Do not undo effective-volume chart/model ranking from PR #14.
- Do not redesign the entire app shell.
- Do not add previous-window deltas unless reliable previous-period data is added separately.

## Acceptance criteria

- Overview includes a `Usage Summary` strip above metric cards.
- Summary strip shows period, total tokens, cache share, top source, top model/share, peak day, and pricing coverage state.
- Metric card order is updated to prioritize token volume and cost before sessions.
- Cost estimate confidence remains visible as a warning when pricing coverage is partial.
- Tool Source cards distinguish `Included in totals` from `Focused` state.
- Chart area shows a focus summary when a source/model is selected.
- Peak day is visible either as chart annotation or summary callout.
- Legend/source interactions are keyboard-accessible and keep selected state synchronized.
- Typography uses sans for UI/prose and mono for numbers/code-oriented data.

## Related

- Follows #20
- Follows PR #22

## Original body

Make worktrees the default working mode so the `main` checkout stays clean and ready to receive merges.

## Why
`AGENTS.md` already said "prefer small reviewable PRs, do not push straight to main," but it had no concrete mechanism for keeping `main` clean. Sessions that touched feature branches often showed `.worktrees/` as untracked in the `main` checkout, and a worktree lived in the in-repo path for the duration of PR 14.

## What
- **AGENTS.md** (Working style): agents must work in a worktree, not the `main` checkout. Default location is outside the repo at `../worktrees/<branch-slug>`, with the worktree-add command shown verbatim.
- **AGENTS.md** (Repo conventions): keep `main` clean; retire worktrees with `git worktree remove`.
- **.gitignore**: add `.worktrees/` as a safety net for agents that use the in-repo path.
- **scripts/review.sh**: refuse to run from `main` unless `REVIEW_MODE=docs`; the error message points the agent at the worktree-add command.
- **tests/test_readme.py**: assert the new AGENTS.md guidance and the `.worktrees/` ignore line.
- **tests/test_app.py**: new `ReviewScriptGuardTests` class exercises the guard with a stubbed `git` binary, so the test stays self-contained and doesn't recurse into the suite it is testing.

- Same call from `main` with `REVIEW_MODE=docs` → exit 0

- Removing the existing in-repo worktree at `.worktrees/review-pr-14`. It pre-dates this rule and will be retired by the user separately.

> Migration source: `raychrisgdp/coding-agent-usage-dashboard` issue #20
> Original author: `raychrisgdp`
> Created: `2026-06-02T04:58:26Z`
> Updated: `2026-06-02T17:01:09Z`
> Original state: `closed`
> Original URL: https://github.com/raychrisgdp/coding-agent-usage-dashboard/issues/20
> Original GitHub timestamps, author identity, reactions, and timeline events are preserved in the private raw archive.

---

## Summary

After PR #14 moved ranking/chart semantics to effective token volume, improve the top-level Overview cards so token accounting is easier to understand at a glance.

The current cards are technically correct, but the primary labels still force readers to mentally reconcile canonical totals, non-cache input, cached input, cache read/write, and effective volume.

## Current UI example

From the 1-day Overview screenshot:

- Page subtitle: `Primary totals use non-cache input + assistant output tokens. Cache read/write is tracked separately.`
- `Total Tokens`: `15.1M`, secondary line `151.6M read / 0 write cache`
- `Non-cache Input`: `14.5M`, secondary line `151.6M cache read`
- `Output Tokens`: `666.4K`, secondary line `0 cache write`

This is accurate by the current data model, but the naming makes the top-level cards feel more like implementation accounting than user-facing analytics.


## Visual framing

### Current state: correct, but hard to parse

```text
┌──────────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────┐
│ TOTAL TOKENS         │  │ NON-CACHE INPUT      │  │ OUTPUT TOKENS        │
│ 15.1M                │  │ 14.5M                │  │ 666.4K               │
│ 151.6M read / 0 write│  │ 151.6M cache read    │  │ 0 cache write        │
└──────────────────────┘  └──────────────────────┘  └──────────────────────┘
```

Problem: the biggest volume (`151.6M cache read`) is visually secondary, while `Total Tokens` sounds like the full number but is actually canonical/fresh-only accounting.

### Token relationship for the screenshot

```text
Effective volume ≈ 166.7M
├─ Fresh input       14.5M   ████
├─ Assistant output  0.7M    ▏
├─ Cache read        151.6M  ████████████████████████████████████████
└─ Cache write       0       

Canonical total = fresh input + output = 15.1M
Effective volume = canonical total + cache read + cache write = 166.7M
Cached share ≈ 91% of effective volume
```

The UI should make this relationship obvious without requiring the user to open tooltips.

## Candidate card layouts

### A. Effective-volume-first layout

Best if Overview should match chart/model ranking.

```text
┌──────────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────┐
│ EFFECTIVE TOKENS     │  │ INPUT TOKENS         │  │ OUTPUT TOKENS        │
│ 166.7M               │  │ 166.1M               │  │ 666.4K               │
│ 15.1M canonical      │  │ 14.5M fresh · 91% cached│ 0 cache write       │
└──────────────────────┘  └──────────────────────┘  └──────────────────────┘
```

### B. Canonical-first layout with explicit cache ratio

Best if AGENTS.md canonical accounting stays primary.

```text
┌──────────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────┐
│ CANONICAL TOKENS     │  │ INPUT TOKENS         │  │ OUTPUT TOKENS        │
│ 15.1M                │  │ 14.5M fresh          │  │ 666.4K               │
│ +151.6M cache · 10.0×│  │ +151.6M cached · 91% │  │ 0 cache write        │
└──────────────────────┘  └──────────────────────┘  └──────────────────────┘
```

### C. Split both totals explicitly

Best if both definitions must be visible as first-class numbers.

```text
┌──────────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────┐
│ CANONICAL TOKENS     │  │ EFFECTIVE TOKENS     │  │ INPUT TOKENS         │  │ OUTPUT TOKENS        │
│ 15.1M                │  │ 166.7M               │  │ 14.5M fresh          │  │ 666.4K               │
│ fresh input + output │  │ incl. 151.6M cache   │  │ 151.6M cached · 91%  │  │ 0 cache write        │
└──────────────────────┘  └──────────────────────┘  └──────────────────────┘  └──────────────────────┘
```

### Copy comparison

| Current label | Issue | Possible replacement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Total Tokens` | Sounds like it includes cache, but it excludes cache | `Canonical Tokens` or `Effective Tokens`, depending on chosen primary model |
| `Non-cache Input` | Accurate but implementation-shaped | `Input Tokens` with `fresh` / `cached` split |
| `151.6M cache read` | Raw number only; scale is not obvious | `151.6M cached · 91% cached` or `+151.6M cache · 10.0× canonical` |
| Page subtitle | Explains the rule, but not the visual hierarchy | `Overview shows canonical totals and cache share; chart ranks by effective volume.` |

## Problem

The top-level view needs to answer two questions without ambiguity:

1. What was the actual token volume represented by this usage, including cached context?
2. What is the canonical non-cache total used by the app's historical/session accounting?

Right now:

- `Total Tokens` looks like the largest/most complete number, but it excludes cache.
- `Non-cache Input` is precise, but too implementation-shaped as a primary card label.
- Cache appears as raw secondary text, but not as a share/ratio, so the scale difference is hard to read. In the screenshot, `151.6M cache read` dwarfs `14.5M non-cache input`, but that relationship is not visually explained.
- The page subtitle says cache is tracked separately, but the chart/model ranking now uses effective volume including cache, so the top-level cards should make that split obvious.

## Desired direction

Prefer a user-facing top-level accounting model:

- Rename `Non-cache Input` to `Input Tokens` unless there is a stronger reason to keep the implementation term in the card title.
- Show the primary input number as either:
  - total input = fresh/non-cache input + cached input, or
  - fresh input as the main number with cached input shown as a prominent secondary ratio.
- Surface cache as both raw tokens and a percentage/share, not only raw text.
- Keep canonical/session totals available, but avoid making `Total Tokens` sound like it includes cache when it does not.

## Design options to evaluate

### Option A: Effective volume first

Top cards emphasize the volume users intuitively expect:

- `Effective Tokens` = canonical total + cache read + cache write
- `Input Tokens` = fresh input + cached input
- secondary line: `14.5M fresh · 151.6M cached · 91% cached`
- `Canonical Total` appears as a smaller secondary line or info tooltip: `15.1M canonical = fresh input + output`

Good when the Overview should align with chart/model ranking.

### Option B: Canonical total first, cache ratio explicit

Keep canonical accounting primary, but make the exclusion impossible to miss:

- `Total Tokens` or `Canonical Tokens` = non-cache input + output
- secondary line: `+151.6M cache read (10.0× canonical)` or `cache read: 91% of effective volume`
- `Input Tokens` = fresh/non-cache input, with secondary `151.6M cached read`

Good when preserving AGENTS.md canonical definitions as the main surface matters more than intuitive volume.

### Option C: Split primary card into two related totals

Use two explicit cards:

- `Canonical Tokens` = fresh input + output
- `Effective Tokens` = canonical + cache read/write

Then input/output cards can be simpler:

- `Input Tokens`: `14.5M fresh · 151.6M cached`
- `Output Tokens`: `666.4K generated · 0 cache write`

Good when the dashboard needs both definitions visible without burying one in tooltips.


## Chosen direction after UI review

Keep the top-level Overview cards in simple product language and push exact accounting into secondary lines/tooltips.

Avoid primary labels such as `Canonical`, `Effective`, and `Fresh Tokens`. They are precise but feel like internal accounting terms. The reference usage/cost/balance dashboards use plain labels such as `Usage`, `Cost`, `Balance`, `Input`, `Output`, `remaining`, and `usage limit` first, then explain details nearby.

### Final top-level labels

```text
Sessions
Total Tokens
Input Tokens
Output Tokens
API-Equivalent Cost
```

Do not add `Fresh Tokens` as a primary card. Use `Session Tokens` only as secondary/detail language.

### Final semantics

```text
Total Tokens   = session tokens + cache read + cache write
Input Tokens   = non-cache input + cache read + cache write
Output Tokens  = assistant output
Session Tokens = non-cache input + assistant output
```

### Recommended card copy pattern

```text
SESSIONS
1,767
2026-05-03 → 2026-06-02

TOTAL TOKENS
776.6M
747.2M session · 10.4B cached

INPUT TOKENS
10.7B
718.2M fresh · 10.4B read · 19.7M write

OUTPUT TOKENS
29.0M
assistant-generated

API-EQUIVALENT COST
$6292.88
approx · 35/64 priced
```

### Rationale

- `Total Tokens` should mean the intuitive full volume users expect.
- `Input Tokens` should replace `Non-cache Input` at card level.
- `Output Tokens` should stay paired with `Input Tokens`; `Generated Tokens` is friendlier but breaks the common billing/usage pair.
- `Session Tokens` is useful detail language for the current canonical/session total, but it should not be a top-level card unless the layout needs it later.
- Cache write should not appear under `Output Tokens`; it is provider-side cached context creation, not assistant output.

## Acceptance criteria

- Overview card titles do not require knowing internal terms like `non-cache` to understand the metric.
- The top-level cards clearly distinguish:
  - fresh/non-cache input
  - cached input/cache read
  - assistant output
  - cache write
  - canonical total
  - effective volume
- If `Total Tokens` remains canonical, the label/subtitle/tooltips make clear that cache is excluded.
- If effective volume becomes primary, canonical total remains visible as secondary context.
- Cache context is shown as raw number plus ratio/share where useful, especially when cache dominates the range.
- Chart/model ranking language stays consistent with the Overview language after PR #14.
- The final copy fits the existing compact dark dashboard card layout and remains readable at the current card widths.

## Non-goals

- Do not change the underlying token data model unless the UI decision requires a missing aggregate field.
- Do not undo PR #14's effective-volume chart/ranking behavior.
- Do not redesign the whole dashboard; keep this scoped to the top-level Overview metric cards and nearby explanatory copy.

## Related

- Follow-up after PR #14 merged: effective-token chart/ranking semantics are now fixed, but top-level Overview wording still needs a product/UX pass.
- Related broader wording issue: #5

## Goal

Fill `EST. COST` for active models that currently show `—` because their local model IDs are not mapped to any registered pricing entry.

## Current behavior

The dashboard estimates cost through `openrouter_model_id()` plus OpenRouter public pricing and a hardcoded fallback map. Models that do not map to a known provider/model ID return `estimated_cost: null`, which renders as `—` in the Model Breakdown table.

Observed live examples with non-trivial token volume:

| Tool | Model label | Provider | Why cost is missing |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| OpenCode | `nemotron-3-super-free` | `opencode` | no pricing alias/mapping |
| OpenCode | `gpt-5.3-codex-spark (openai)` | `openai` | no OpenRouter/hardcoded pricing entry |
| Hermes | `gpt-5.3-codex-spark` | `openai-codex` | no pricing entry for Codex provider alias |
| OpenCode | `mimo-v2.5-free` | `opencode` | no pricing alias/mapping |
| OpenCode | `antigravity-gemini-3-flash` | `google` | no pricing alias/mapping |
| OpenCode | `antigravity-gemini-3.1-pro` | `google` | no pricing alias/mapping |
| OpenCode | `antigravity-gemini-3.1-pro-low` | `google` | no pricing alias/mapping |

These rows can represent millions of tokens, so leaving them as `—` makes the total cost view incomplete.

## Proposed approach

Create a maintainable pricing alias registry instead of growing ad hoc conditionals in `openrouter_model_id()`.

Suggested shape:

- canonical provider/model ID
- local aliases seen in OpenCode, Codex, Hermes, Antigravity, etc.
- pricing source priority
- cache read/write price support
- status: priced / intentionally free / unknown / needs manual mapping

Example behavior:

- `provider=openai`, `model_id=gpt-5.3-codex-spark` maps to the correct billable OpenAI/Codex Spark price if available.
- `provider=openai-codex`, `model_id=gpt-5.3-codex-spark` maps to the same canonical pricing entry as the OpenCode OpenAI row when appropriate.
- Antigravity Gemini aliases map to their canonical Gemini SKU or remain clearly `unpriced` with a reason.
- Free-suffixed third-party aliases map through the subscription-aware pricing rules from the related free-tier pricing issue, rather than blindly zeroing them out.

## Acceptance criteria

- `EST. COST` is no longer `—` for the highest-volume unmapped models when a trustworthy price exists.
- Pricing aliases are stored in one obvious registry/table, not scattered across route code.
- The API response includes enough metadata to explain missing cost, for example `pricing_status`, `pricing_model_id`, and `pricing_source`.
- The UI can distinguish `unmapped`, `unpriced`, and `intentionally free` instead of rendering all missing cases as an unexplained dash.
- Add tests for at least these mapping classes:
  - OpenAI Codex Spark alias from OpenCode
  - OpenAI Codex Spark alias from Hermes/Codex provider naming
  - one Antigravity Gemini alias
  - one third-party free-suffixed alias that remains unresolved until subscription-aware pricing is available

---

## Goal

Fill `EST. COST` for models that are currently displayed as free/zero-cost when the active API key or subscription may imply a real billable price.

## Current behavior

The pricing layer currently maps some free-suffixed model IDs to zero-cost hardcoded pricing, for example:

- `deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash:free` → `$0.00`
- `deepseek-v4-flash-free` → `$0.00`
- `minimax-m2.5-free` → `$0.00`

This is correct only when the actual execution path used a free tier. If the request was served under a paid/subscribed API key, provider account, or non-free alias, the dashboard should prefer the actual billable price instead of assuming zero from the display/model suffix.

## Problem

The current cost estimate can understate usage when:

- a local tool stores a `*-free` or `:free` model label, but the provider/API key routes to a paid/subscribed plan
- OpenRouter or another provider exposes free public list pricing, while the user's key has account-specific/subscription pricing
- the local session record has enough provider/model/account metadata to resolve a paid price, but the dashboard collapses it to the public free alias

Observed high-impact examples from the live dashboard:

| Tool | Model label | Current EST. COST behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hermes | `deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash:free` | `$0.00` |
| OpenCode | `deepseek-v4-flash-free` | `$0.00` |
| OpenCode | `minimax-m2.5-free` | `$0.00` |

## Proposed approach

Add a pricing resolution layer that can distinguish:

1. public free-tier price
2. provider/account/API-key-specific price, when available
3. explicitly unpriced/unknown price

Implementation options:

- If a provider exposes account/API-key-specific pricing, fetch it with the configured key and prefer it over public `/models` pricing.
- Preserve the public OpenRouter price as a fallback, but tag the source clearly.
- Keep `free` labels visible as model labels, but do not make `free` imply `$0.00` unless the price source proves it.
- Add a `pricing_source` or equivalent UI hint such as `OpenRouter public`, `provider/account`, `hardcoded fallback`, or `unpriced`.

## Acceptance criteria

- Free-suffixed models do not automatically show `$0.00` unless the selected pricing source confirms zero.
- When an API-key/subscription-aware price can be resolved, `EST. COST` uses that price.
- The model breakdown row exposes whether the price came from account-specific pricing, public pricing, or fallback pricing.
- If no account-specific price can be retrieved, the UI remains honest: public free price and unknown/subscription ambiguity are distinguishable.
- Add regression coverage for at least one `:free` model and one `-free` model where account-specific pricing overrides the zero fallback.

Part of #1.
issues.title: Use API-key/subscription-aware pricing before treating free models as $0

---

## Problem

The dashboard now has multiple tool sources, e.g. OpenCode and Codex CLI, but chart filtering is still model-first and feels weird when combined with tool/source selection.

Current confusing paths:

- Clicking a Tool Source card/name filters the chart by tool, but the Model Breakdown table below still shows every tool.
- Clicking `Focus chart` in Model Breakdown switches from a tool filter to a model filter and clears the tool context.
- Clicking model legend items on the right only hides/shows chart series, which is visually useful but is a different interaction from filtering.
- The UI does not clearly distinguish source/tool filters from chart-series visibility toggles.

This becomes more obvious once `gpt-5.5 (openai)` appears under both OpenCode and Codex CLI: users may expect to filter by tool, by model, or by tool+model, but the current controls collapse those meanings.

## Desired outcome

Make tool filtering explicit, predictable, and available for both the chart and Model Breakdown table.

At minimum:

- Users can filter Model Breakdown by tool: OpenCode, Codex CLI, Hermes when available, or All.
- The active tool filter is visible near the chart/table, not only implied by a source card state.
- Model chart focus and tool filter do not unexpectedly erase each other unless the UI clearly says so.
- Legend hide/show behavior is visually separated from semantic filtering.

## Possible alternatives

### Alternative A — Global Tool filter chips

Add a persistent filter row near the range tabs:

- `All tools`
- `OpenCode`
- `Codex CLI`
- future `Hermes`

This filter applies to:

- overview totals
- Daily Tokens chart
- Model Breakdown
- Usage History

Pros:

- Most predictable mental model.
- One source of truth for tool scope.
- Makes screenshots and summaries easier to interpret.

Cons:

- Changes overview totals behavior, so the UI must clearly show when totals are scoped.
- Requires more API support if every endpoint accepts `tool_id`.

### Alternative B — Chart-only source focus + table tool tabs

Keep Tool Source cards as chart controls, but add tool tabs directly above Model Breakdown:

- `All`
- `OpenCode`
- `Codex CLI`

Pros:

- Smallest UX change.
- Avoids changing overview totals.
- Lets Model Breakdown answer the immediate comparison problem.

Cons:

- Two different tool filters can diverge: one for chart, one for table.
- Still requires careful copy explaining why chart and table may not match.

### Alternative C — Combined filter state: Tool + Model

Allow both filters at once:

- tool filter: `Codex CLI`
- model filter: `gpt-5.5 (openai)`

Chart and table both apply the intersection. Add visible filter pills with remove buttons:

`Tool: Codex CLI ×` `Model: gpt-5.5 (openai) ×`

Pros:

- Most powerful and precise.
- Handles duplicated model names across tools cleanly.
- Better long-term if the dashboard will add Hermes or other coding agents.

Cons:

- More state complexity.
- Needs careful empty states and accessibility handling.

### Alternative D — Separate legend toggles from filter actions

Keep chart legend as visibility-only, but rename/annotate it:

- Legend title: `Show/hide chart series`
- Model Breakdown button: `Filter dashboard`
- Source card button: `Filter by tool`

Pros:

- Clarifies current behavior with minimal structural changes.
- Reduces surprise when clicking legend items.

Cons:

- Does not solve Model Breakdown filtering by itself.
- Still leaves mixed chart/table scope unless paired with A, B, or C.

## Recommendation

## Goal

Extend the local usage dashboard beyond OpenCode so it can compare usage across coding-agent tools.

This is the umbrella issue for the shared dashboard/data-model work. Tool-specific source adapters are split into separate issues so Codex and Hermes can be implemented and validated independently.

## Split implementation issues

- #3 — Add Codex usage source adapter
- #4 — Add Hermes usage source adapter

## Current baseline

- OpenCode usage from `~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db` is the active source.
- PR #2 prepares the dashboard framing/UI for cross-tool usage but does not implement Codex or Hermes source adapters.

## Proposed product shape

Add a tool dimension to the data model and UI:

- Tool filter: OpenCode / Codex / Hermes / All tools
- Per-tool overview cards: sessions, total tokens, input tokens, output tokens
- Daily stacked chart grouped by top N model/tool series, with long tail grouped as Other
- Model breakdown table with tool, provider, model, sessions, total/input/output tokens
- Usage history table with tool, date, model, title/session summary, tokens

## Design notes

- Keep colors categorical and position-based in charts, not hardcoded per model, because the top models can vary by date range and tool.
- Keep long-tail series grouped into Other after top 6-8 visible series.
- Treat cache/cost as secondary unless explicitly selected.
- Avoid claiming parity across tools until the local data quality is verified for each source.
- Do not silently treat missing/unavailable tool data as zero usage.

## Implementation notes

Use a source adapter layer:

```text
sources/
  opencode.py
  codex.py   # tracked by #3
  hermes.py  # tracked by #4
```

Each adapter should normalize into a common record shape:

```text
tool, session_id, timestamp, title, provider, model, input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_read, cache_write
```

- Dashboard can show OpenCode-only exactly as today.
- Shared data model supports multiple tools without breaking existing OpenCode metrics.
- Missing/unavailable Codex or Hermes data is shown clearly, not silently treated as zero usage.
- Chart and table order stay consistent: same top-N order, same position colors, Other muted gray.
